summary: Lays out design considerations for what became version 4 of the Network File System, presenting the areas the working group planned to investigate, in more detail than its charter. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A planning memo from a team about to redesign how computers share files over a network, listing the problems they want to solve first.

subtitle: Planning the redesign of the Network File System for Internet use with strong security and better performance.

tldr.problem: NFS versions 2 and 3 have limitations: weak security, Unix-centric design, poor Internet performance, unreliable file locking, and difficulty supporting multiple platforms.
tldr.mechanism: This design document outlines investigation areas for NFS version 4: extensibility and versioning, reliable failover, scalable performance with client caching, cross-platform interoperability, strong authentication and security negotiation, Internet accessibility, integrated file locking, and internationalization support.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a planning framework that guided the development of NFS version 4, which later became a major Internet standard for distributed file systems.

today: This document served as a planning framework for NFS version 4, which was later published in RFC 3010 (2000) and RFC 7530 (2015), becoming a widely-deployed Internet standard.

sections.title: Design Goals and Extensibility
sections.content:
NFS version 4 aims to improve on versions 2 and 3 by focusing on Internet use, strong security with protocol-level negotiation, better cross-platform support, and protocol extensibility. A key goal is to avoid the burden of changing RPC version numbers for minor protocol improvements, which has historically slowed protocol evolution. The document proposes mechanisms for managed extensions or minor versioning to allow new procedures, attributes, and file types to be added without full protocol revision.

The working group recognizes that NFS's traditional strength—simplicity of design and implementation—must be preserved while addressing fundamental limitations. NFS version 4 will be self-contained and independent of earlier versions, not requiring previous NFS implementations to be present for functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The team wants to make NFS better for the Internet while keeping it relatively simple. They plan to allow small improvements without having to redesign everything each time.

sections.title: Reliability, Availability, and Performance
sections.content:
NFS version 4 should support client failover to server replicas more cleanly than versions 2 and 3. The RFC notes that NFS currently requires file handles to be immutable, which complicates failover and high-availability configurations. The new protocol should relax or reconsider this requirement to ease implementation of layered reliability solutions.

For performance, the protocol must address network latency and throughput. While NFS 3 improved on NFS 2 by returning attributes with most operations to reduce GETATTR requests, further optimization is needed. The protocol should enable batching multiple RPC operations together, similar to CIFS 'batched requests', to reduce round-trip latency in high-latency Internet environments. Aggressive client-side caching with server callback mechanisms (like AFS and DCE/DFS use) should be explored to reduce network traffic and server load.
sections.plainLanguage: The team wants clients to switch to backup servers more easily if the main server fails. They also want to reduce the number of back-and-forth messages between computers to make the network faster.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Interoperability
sections.content:
NFS versions 2 and 3 have Unix-centric design that makes implementation difficult on other platforms. NFS version 4 must address platform-specific issues: persistent file handles that work across servers, string-based user identification instead of Unix numeric user IDs, support for extended and named attributes, Access Control Lists (ACLs) compatible with multiple platforms, and Unicode support for internationalization.

The RFC discusses the complexity of supporting ACLs across different operating environments (POSIX, DCE/DFS, Windows NT), which define entry types, identity mappings, and permission bits differently. Despite this complexity, basic ACL support is necessary. For internationalization, the document proposes using Unicode and UTF-8 encoding for file and directory names and symlink contents, replacing NFS 2 and 3's 7-bit ASCII limitation.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS was designed for Unix computers, which makes it hard to use with Windows or Mac systems. The new version needs to support fancy permission systems and multiple languages.

sections.title: Security and User Identification
sections.content:
NFS version 4 must provide strong authentication, data integrity, and optional data privacy. Previous versions relied on weak security mechanisms (AUTH_SYS or AUTH_DH), with RPCSEC_GSS being the first to provide real security. The new version should support both public-key and private-key mechanisms through RPCSEC_GSS or similar frameworks, while allowing transport independence (UDP and TCP).

User identification should move from numeric Unix UIDs to string-based identifiers that can integrate with external naming services and handle multiple administrative domains. This enables flexibility for environments with complex identity management. Critically, security mechanism negotiation must be part of the protocol itself, allowing clients and servers to agree on acceptable mechanisms. Different parts of the file system may require different security levels, requiring negotiation at file system boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The new NFS needs real security with strong passwords and encryption. Instead of just numbers for usernames, it should use text names that can work with company directory systems.

sections.title: Internet Accessibility and File Locking
sections.content:
For Internet use, NFS must work through firewalls and handle high-latency environments. The protocol should support proxy/cache servers and firewall traversal. TCP should be the primary transport with proper congestion control, though UDP may be retained if congestion control can be resolved. File locking, which was provided by the separate Network Lock Manager (NLM) protocol in earlier NFS versions, should be integrated into NFS version 4 itself. Separate protocols complicate implementation and testing, leading to poor interoperability. The new integrated locking must be Internet-capable (no server-initiated callbacks), support both Unix and PC semantics, be scalable to thousands of clients, and provide fast recovery from failures.

Internationalization support extends to directory and file naming, allowing NFS to work effectively in multilingual environments. The RFC emphasizes that these Internet accessibility features must be considered during protocol development to avoid retrofitting them later.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS needs to work well on the Internet through security barriers and with poor connections. File locking (preventing two people from changing the same file) should be built in, not added later.
